item.title: Seattle Public Schools will revise policies and procedures to ensure it provides pregnancy accommodations following AG suit
item.description:
Seattle Public Schools will revise policies and procedures to ensure it provides pregnancy accommodations following AG suit
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:
Nov 23 2026
atgSamBlobaum Mon, 11/23/2026 - 09:00

The Attorney General’s Office reached a settlement with Seattle Public schools Friday resolving allegations that the district repeatedly failed to provide reasonable accommodations to pregnant and nursing employees as required by state law.

The consent decree requires Seattle Public Schools to give their employees pregnancy accommodations as required by law and establish new policies and training to ensure that schools follow the law in the future.

“Under state law, employers must provide reasonable accommodations to pregnant and nursing employees,” said Attorney General Nick Brown. “This agreement will ensure that pregnant and nursing teachers and school employees receive the protections they are entitled to under the law.” 

The AG’s office sued Seattle Public Schools in 2025 following an investigation which found schools failed to provide legally required accommodations to pregnant and nursing employees such as flexible restroom breaks, modified work schedules, the ability to sit more frequently, and the ability to express breastmilk in a clean and private location. 

Other employees alleged that they were retaliated against for seeking accommodations and admonished for having doctors’ appointments.

These practices affected employees across various Seattle Public Schools campuses over several years. The state’s investigation revealed Seattle Public Schools did not have a district-level policy for how to handle pregnancy accommodation requests from employees.

The settlement will address these issues. Under the settlement, Seattle Public Schools can’t refuse to provide legally required accommodations for pregnant employees, such as allowing an employee to sit more frequently and providing reasonable break time and a private location for employees to express breast milk. The district will also clearly inform employees that they will not face retaliation for requesting accommodations. 

Seattle Public Schools must also institute a district-wide policy on pregnancy accommodations. This policy will lay out clear expectations for how Seattle Public Schools is to handle accommodation requests in a way that complies with Washington law. Under the new policy, the district will respond to employee requests for accommodation within five business days. The district must also train the employees responsible for reviewing pregnancy accommodation requests to ensure they understand how to comply with the law.

Seattle Public Schools will also pay $600,000 into a fund that the AG’s office will use to compensate affected workers, enforce the consent decree, and recover costs as needed.

Assistant Attorneys General Alfredo González Benítez and Daniel Jeon, former Assistant Attorneys General Diane Lopez and David Ward, as well as investigator Jennifer Sievert, and Paralegal Panda Halford handled the case for Washington.

Healthy Starts Act

Washington’s Healthy Starts Act, which went into effect in July 2017, provides significant pregnancy-related rights under Washington law. The law requires employers—with limited exceptions—to make reasonable pregnancy-related accommodations, including:

  • Providing more frequent, longer, or flexible restroom breaks.
  • Modifying a no food or drink policy.
  • Job restructuring, part-time or modified work schedules, reassignment to a vacant position, or acquiring or modifying equipment, devices, or an employee’s workstation.
  • Providing seating or allowing the employee to sit more frequently if their job requires them to stand.
  • Providing for a temporary transfer to a less strenuous or less hazardous position.
  • Providing assistance with manual labor and limits on lifting.
  • Scheduling flexibility for prenatal visits.
  • Providing reasonable break time and a private location other than the school bathroom to express breast milk for up to two years after the child's birth when the employee has need to express the milk.
  • Any further pregnancy accommodation an employee may request, and to which an employer must give reasonable consideration.

Additional information about the Healthy Starts Act is available on the AGO website: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding Accommodations. Workers who have experienced pregnancy related discrimination or retaliation may also submit a complaint using an online form or by calling 1-833-660-4877.

Read the consent decree.

item.title: Washington joins coalition suing to protect housing assistance for mixed-status families
item.description:
Washington joins coalition suing to protect housing assistance for mixed-status families
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:
Nov 23 2026
atgAshleyGross Mon, 11/23/2026 - 08:45

A new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule would unlawfully strip federal housing assistance from mixed-status families, according to a new lawsuit filed by Washington and 22 other plaintiffs.

Under the new rule, any household with at least one member who is not eligible for housing assistance due to their immigration status would be cut off from HUD assistance entirely, even though federal subsidies are already prorated to only include eligible individuals in those households. The change means about 600 mixed-status families in Washington face the prospect of losing their homes or having to split up. The rule is expected to heavily impact children, with HUD’s own analysis estimating that 65% of eligible members of mixed-status families are under the age of 18. 

“Because of this unlawful rule, hundreds of Washington families face homelessness,” Attorney General Nick Brown said. “Our office will fight this administration’s cruel attempt to upend federal housing policy so we can keep families in Washington stable and defend the rule of law.”

The rule also imposes a sweeping requirement that all U.S. citizens in federal housing programs undertake additional and potentially burdensome steps to once again establish their eligibility or risk eviction. In Washington, about 82,000 people who have already demonstrated their eligibility would be subject to these new requirements. 

Under the new rule, every U.S. citizen would also need to provide their Social Security number and consent to have their citizenship status checked through the federal SAVE database. If SAVE cannot automatically confirm their citizenship, U.S. citizens would have to produce official documents to prove their status, such as an original or certified birth certificate, naturalization certificate, or passport. 

In a lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, Brown and the coalition argue that the rule illegally reverses nearly 30 years of federal policy, and clear Congressional intent, allowing mixed-status families to stay together and violates the Administrative Procedure Act by exceeding HUD’s authority to enact this arbitrary new restriction. 

For nearly 30 years, federal housing programs have provided housing assistance to low-income families even if not every household member is eligible for assistance. Under this system, known as proration, HUD reduces the family’s subsidy so it covers only the eligible household members. Congress codified this protection in 1997, explicitly stating that families receiving prorated assistance “shall not” lose their benefits just because an ineligible family member lives with them. The new HUD rule eliminates this protection. 

Under the administration’s new rule, a family can stay in HUD-assisted housing only if every household member is a U.S. citizen or an eligible immigrant. As a result, U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants who live with an ineligible relative will be forced to choose between maintaining their housing and keeping their family together. 

Nationwide, HUD estimates that around 20,000 mixed-status families, totaling 78,100 people, will lose their housing assistance. This includes 55,000 people who are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, many of whom are children and seniors. The agency also acknowledges that the rule will lead to evictions and displacement, and that many of these families could become homeless.   

The coalition asserts that the rule will increase homelessness and shift major costs onto state and local governments. By HUD’s own estimates, sheltering people displaced by the rule could cost governments between $20,000 and $50,000 per person each year. 

Brown and the coalition argue that HUD’s new rule exceeds the agency’s authority and violates federal law, which expressly allows prorated assistance for mixed-status families and establishes different documentation requirements for U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants aged 62 and older. They argue that HUD also violated the Administrative Procedure Act by issuing an arbitrary and capricious rule. The coalition is asking the court to declare the rule unlawful, strike it down, and block HUD from implementing or enforcing it against the plaintiff states, their local governments, and their public housing authorities. 

Joining Brown in filing this lawsuit, which is led by the attorneys general of New York, California, and Massachusetts, are the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaiʻi, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Wisconsin, the District of Columbia, and the governor of Pennsylvania.

item.title: Consejos para que los habitantes de Washington detecten fraude en organizaciones benéficas durante esta temporada de donaciones
item.description:
Consejos para que los habitantes de Washington detecten fraude en organizaciones benéficas durante esta temporada de donaciones
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:
Nov 18 2026
atgAshleyGross Wed, 11/18/2026 - 09:47

Charity fraud awareness tips for Washingtonians during this giving season

Mientras los habitantes de Washington buscan formas de hacer donaciones caritativas en esta época del año, es ideal investigar las causas para detectar posibles estafas antes de donar.

Esta semana se celebra la Semana Internacional de Concientización sobre el Fraude Caritativo (solo en inglés), época en la que la Oficina del Procurador General (AGO, por sus siglas en inglés) y la Oficina de la Secretaría de Estado colaboran para brindarle a los habitantes de Washington consejos sobre cómo donar de manera segura y evitar las solicitudes de donaciones benéficas engañosas o fraudulentas. 

El tema de la campaña es “Tómese un momento y verifique la causa”.

Tomarse un momento antes de donar les permite a las personas evitar dar de manera impulsiva y convertirse en víctimas de solicitudes que podrían ser estafas. Verifique la causa es un recordatorio para investigar con el fin de asegurarse de que la organización esté exenta de impuestos y se encuentre registrada como organización benéfica en la Oficina de la Secretaría de Estado (solo en inglés).

“Queremos fomentar la generosidad y el compromiso de ayudar a los demás que tanto caracterizan a los habitantes de Washington”, indicó el procurador general Nick Brown. “Siga estos consejos para asegurarse de que su donación se destine a la organización benéfica que quiere apoyar y, en caso de encontrarse con una posible estafa, denúnciela a nuestra oficina”.

“Las organizaciones benéficas auténticas se esfuerzan para demostrar que el dinero donado realmente se destine a beneficiar a las personas que lo necesitan”, indicó el secretario Steve Hobbs. “Mi oficina cuenta con la información que necesita para asegurarse de que su dinero realmente se destine a una buena causa”.

Si va a donar a organizaciones sin fines de lucro u organizaciones benéficas, nuestra oficina le ofrece algunos consejos sobre cómo asegurarse de que su donación beneficie a quienes desea ayudar: 

  • Investigue antes de donar. Las organizaciones benéficas deben registrarse en la Oficina de la Secretaría de Estado (solo en inglés). El registro de una organización benéfica no supone el respaldo de la Oficina de la Secretaría de Estado, pero puede utilizarse para obtener información básica, como la ubicación de la organización y el porcentaje que destina a sus fines benéficos. 
  • Las tácticas de presión son una señal de alarma. Tenga cuidado con las peticiones insistentes de donaciones inmediatas o con aquellas en las que se solicite información personal confidencial. Podrían tratarse de una estafa.
  • Tenga cuidado con los impostores. Las organizaciones fraudulentas pueden utilizar nombres muy parecidos a los de organizaciones benéficas reconocidas para engañar a los donantes. Tenga cuidado con los sitios web fraudulentos cuya dirección web difiera ligeramente de la de una organización benéfica legítima. 
  • Tenga cuidado con los códigos QR. Los códigos QR son una forma rápida de ingresar a un sitio web o a una aplicación, pero los estafadores pueden utilizarlos para redirigirlo a campañas de recaudación de fondos falsas o a sitios web maliciosos. Escanee únicamente códigos QR de fuentes fiables o de remitentes conocidos. Compruebe siempre la dirección URL que aparece en la pantalla antes de hacer clic en ella y asegúrese de que empiece con “https”.  
  • Proteja su información de pago. No dé su información bancaria por teléfono ni al responder un correo electrónico o mensaje de texto. Evite usar métodos de tecnología sin contacto para donar. 
  • Apoye organizaciones benéficas de confianza. Considere donar a organizaciones benéficas reconocidas en lugar de apoyar campañas de financiamiento colectivo. 
  • Denuncie los posibles casos de estafas. Presente una queja ante la AGO si se encuentra con una solicitud sospechosa. 

También les pedimos a los consumidores de Washington que recuerden estos consejos, sobre todo después de tragedias de gran repercusión, cuando la gente suele apresurarse a ayudar sin investigar lo suficiente para verificar la veracidad de una solicitud de ayuda. A principios de este año, la AGO advirtió a los consumidores que se tomaran el tiempo necesario para estar atentos a las solicitudes fraudulentas de donaciones a organizaciones benéficas tras los devastadores incendios en Spokane y el desastre de la fábrica de papel de Longview (solo en inglés).

-30-

El Procurador General de Washington sirve al pueblo y al estado de Washington. Como la oficina judicial más grande de Washington, la Oficina del Procurador General brinda representación legal a todas las agencias, juntas y comisiones estatales de Washington. Además, la oficina sirve directamente a la gente al hacer cumplir las leyes de protección de los consumidores, de derechos civiles y de protección al medioambiente. La oficina también persigue el abuso de personas mayores, el fraude de Medicaid, y atiende los casos de depredadores sexuales violentos en 38 de los 39 condados de Washington. Para obtener más información, visite www.atg.wa.gov.

item.title: Charity fraud awareness tips for Washingtonians during this giving season
item.description:
Charity fraud awareness tips for Washingtonians during this giving season
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:
Nov 18 2026
atgAshleyGross Wed, 11/18/2026 - 09:35

Consejos para que los habitantes de Washington detecten fraude en organizaciones benéficas durante esta temporada de donaciones

As Washingtonians seek ways to give charitable donations this time of year, they should consider ways to research causes for potential scams before donating.
 
This week is International Charity Fraud Awareness Week, a time when the Attorney General’s Office (AGO) and the Office of the Secretary of State collaborate to share tips with Washingtonians about how to donate safely and avoid deceptive or fraudulent charity solicitations.
 
The campaign’s theme is “Pause. Check the Cause.”
 
Pausing before donating allows people to avoid giving impulsively and falling victim to solicitations that could be scams. Checking the cause is a reminder to do research to make sure the organization is tax-exempt and registered as a charity with the Secretary of State.
 
“We want to encourage the generosity and commitment to helping others that Washingtonians are known for,” Attorney General Nick Brown said. “Follow these tips to help ensure your donation goes to the charity you want to support. And if you encounter a possible scam, please report it to our office.”
 
“Real charities put in the work to prove that donated money is actually going to benefit those in need," said Secretary Steve Hobbs. "My office has the information you need to make sure your money is actually going toward a good cause."
 
If you are giving to non-profits or charities, our office has some tips for how to make sure your donation is benefiting those you want to help: 

  • Research before giving. Charities must register with the Secretary of State’s Office. A charity’s registration is not an endorsement by the Secretary of State, but the registration can be used to find basic information, including the organization's location and what percentage it spends on its charitable purpose. 
  • High-pressure tactics are a red flag. Treat high-pressure asks for immediate donations or ones that request sensitive personal information with caution. They may be a scam.
  • Watch out for imposters. Fraudulent organizations may use names that closely resemble those of well-established charitable organizations to mislead donors. Look out for fraudulent websites that have a slightly different web address than that of a legitimate charitable organization. 
  • Use caution with QR codes. QR codes are a quick way to visit a website or app, but scammers can use them to send you to fake fundraisers or malicious websites. Only scan QR codes from trusted sources or known senders. Always verify the URL displayed on your screen before clicking on it and make sure it starts with “https.”  
  • Protect payment information. Don’t give banking information over the phone or in response to an email or text. Avoid using tap-to-pay to donate.
  • Support trusted charities. Consider donating to established charities instead of crowdfunding appeals.
  • Report suspected scams. File a complaint with the AGO if you encounter suspicious solicitation.

We also urge Washington consumers to remember these tips particularly after high-profile tragedies, when people may rush to help without doing sufficient research to vet a solicitation. Earlier this year, the AGO warned consumers to take time to be on the lookout for fraudulent charity solicitations in the aftermath of destructive fires in Spokane and the Longview paper mill disaster.
